text: Shonda Lynn Rhimes, born January 13, 1970, is an American television producer and screenwriter, and the founder of the production company Shondaland. Inducted into both the Television Hall of Fame and the NAB Broadcasting Hall of Fame, Rhimes became the first showrunner–creator, head writer, and executive producer of the medical drama Grey's Anatomy (2005–present), its spin-off Private Practice (2007–2013), and the political thriller Scandal (2012–2018), making her the first woman to create three television dramas that have reached the 100-episode milestone. She has served as executive producer of the ABC thriller series How to Get Away with Murder (2014–2020), the Netflix period series Bridgerton (2020–present) and Queen Charlotte: A Bridgerton Story (2023), and the drama Inventing Anna (2022). Rhimes has been nominated five times for a Primetime Emmy Award, won a Golden Globe Award and a Daytime Emmy Award, and received special honors at the British Academy Television Awards and the International Emmy Awards. In 2017, she was inducted as a Chair's Appointee of the Academy of Television Arts & Sciences’s executive committee. She is also part of the USC Film Council and the Writers Guild Inclusion Committee. Named by Time to the Time 100 in 2007, 2013, and 2021, Rhimes is one of the richest women entertainers in America with a net worth of $250 million as of 2023. In 2015, she published her memoir, Year of Yes: How to Dance It Out, Stand in the Sun, and Be Your Own Person. In 2016, she formed The Rhimes Family Foundation to support arts, education, and activism. Born in Chicago, Illinois, the youngest of six children, Rhimes’ mother, Vera P. (née Cain), earned a PhD in educational administration in 1991 while raising the family, and her father, Ilee Rhimes Jr., served as a university administrator and became chief information officer at the University of Southern California, a position he held until 2013. Rhimes lived in Park Forest South (now University Park, Illinois) with her two older brothers and three older sisters, and has said she exhibited an early affinity for storytelling. While in high school, she volunteered at a hospital, which inspired her interest in hospital environments. Raised Catholic, she attended Marian Catholic High School in Chicago Heights, Illinois. At Dartmouth College, she majored in English and film studies, earning her bachelor's degree in 1991, and joined the Black Underground Theater Association, where she directed, performed, and wrote fiction, also writing for the college newspaper. After college, she moved to San Francisco with an older sibling and worked in advertising at McCann Erickson, then relocated to Los Angeles to attend the University of Southern California and study screenwriting. Ranked at the top of her USC class, she earned the Gary Rosenberg Writing Fellowship and obtained a Master of Fine Arts degree from the USC School of Cinematic Arts. While at USC, she was hired as an intern by Debra Martin Chase, a prominent African-American producer, who later mentored her on The Princess Diaries 2; she also worked at Denzel Washington's company, Mundy Lane Entertainment. After graduation, Rhimes was unemployed as a scriptwriter in Hollywood and worked various day jobs, including as an office administrator and counselor at a job center for people with housing instability and mental illness. During this time, she served as research director on the documentary Hank Aaron: Chasing the Dream (1995), which won the 1995 Peabody Award. In 1998, she made a short film, Blossoms and Veils, starring Jada Pinkett-Smith and Jeffrey Wright, her only film as a director, and New Line Cinema purchased a feature script of hers. She was assigned to co-write the HBO movie Introducing Dorothy Dandridge (1999), which earned numerous awards for Halle Berry. In 2001, Rhimes wrote Crossroads, the debut film of pop singer Britney Spears, which grossed over $60 million worldwide despite critical panning. She next wrote Disney's sequel to The Princess Diaries (2001), The Princess Diaries 2: Royal Engagement (2004), which did not perform well at the box office but she later valued the experience for working with Julie Andrews. In 2003, she wrote her first TV pilot for ABC about young female war correspondents, which was rejected. Rhimes is the creator and current executive producer and head writer of Grey's Anatomy, which debuted as a mid-season replacement on March 27, 2005, featuring the surgical staff at the fictional Seattle Grace Hospital (later named Grey Sloan Memorial Hospital) in Seattle, Washington, with an ensemble cast including Ellen Pompeo as titular character Meredith Grey, who provides narration for most episodes. In 2007, she created and produced the spin-off Private Practice, which premiered on September 26, 2007, on ABC, chronicling Dr. Addison Montgomery (Kate Walsh) as she moves from Seattle Grace to a private practice in Los Angeles, featuring an ensemble cast including Tim Daly, Amy Brenneman, Audra McDonald, and Taye Diggs. The first season was shortened due to a writers' strike with nine episodes; in May 2012, ABC picked it up for a 13-episode season, concluding on January 22, 2013. In 2010, Rhimes created a pilot for ABC called Inside the Box, a female-centric ensemble drama set in a Washington, D.C. network news bureau with lead character Catherine, an ambitious news producer who pursues stories while managing personal conflicts; the network did not pick it up. In 2011, she served as executive producer for Off the Map, a medical drama created by Grey's Anatomy writer Jenna Bans, focusing on doctors practicing in a remote Amazon jungle clinic, which was officially cancelled by ABC on May 13, 2011. In May 2011, ABC ordered Rhimes' pilot Scandal to series, starring Kerry Washington as Olivia Pope, a political crisis management expert partially based on former Bush administration press aide Judy Smith; the series premiered on April 5, 2012. In 2012, Rhimes developed a pilot for a period drama, Gilded Lilys, which was not picked up. In December 2013, ABC ordered a pilot for How to Get Away with Murder; Viola Davis joined the cast in February 2014, and the series was officially picked up on May 8, 2014. In March 2016, ABC premiered The Catch, a comedy-drama led by Rhimes based on a treatment by Kate Atkinson, starring Mireille Enos and Peter Krause; later that month, Scandal, How to Get Away with Murder, and Grey's Anatomy were picked up for their sixth, third, and 13th seasons, with Scandal announced to conclude after its seventh season and The Catch cancelled after its second. On August 14, 2017, Netflix announced an exclusive multi-year development deal with Rhimes, under which all her future productions would be Netflix Original series; the service had already acquired streaming rights to past episodes of Grey's Anatomy and Scandal. Chief Content Officer Ted Sarandos described Rhimes as a "true Netflixer at heart" because she loves TV and films, cares passionately about her work, and delivers for her audience. The deal was seen as a coup for Netflix due to Rhimes' prominence at ABC and as a counter to Disney, ABC's parent company, seeking to reduce content availability on Netflix in favor of its own streaming service. As of October 2020, she was working on more than 12 projects for Netflix. In July 2021, Rhimes extended her deal with Netflix. The first production was Bridgerton, released in 2020 and becoming the most-watched series ever on the platform, leading to three seasons by 2024. In 2021, Rhimes produced the drama miniseries Inventing Anna. In April 2022, the production of Queen Charlotte: A Bridgerton Story, conceived by Rhimes as a spin-off of Bridgerton, was announced. Rhimes won her first competitive Emmy Award at the 52nd Daytime Creative Arts & Lifestyle Emmy Awards for Outstanding Arts and Popular Culture Program for Black Barbie: A Documentary (2023). She adopted her first daughter in June 2002 and another in February 2012; in September 2013, she welcomed her third daughter via gestational surrogacy. In 2014, she delivered a commencement address at Dartmouth College, where she received an honorary doctorate. In September 2015, Rhimes revealed she had lost 117 pounds (53 kg) through exercise and dieting. In April 2017, she joined the national board of Planned Parenthood. Later that year, she and Katie McGrath co-founded Time's Up, and both donated funds to hire its first seven employees. In 2019, Rhimes joined When We All Vote as a co-chair, an organization founded to get out the vote prior to the 2020 general election. Shondaland is Rhimes' production company, and the name and logo also refer to the shows she has produced and to Rhimes herself. Shows included in Shondaland are: Grey's Anatomy, which won the Golden Globe Award for Best Television Series – Drama in 2006, and Rhimes received the International Emmy Founders Award and the Special Award at the British Academy Television Awards. She also received special honorees at the Costume Designers Guild Awards, Directors Guild of America Award, ICG Publicists Awards, Writers Guild of America Award, and Producers Guild of America Awards.
